entry.evidence: In contrast, the causes behind snow depth change are still inconclusive, as the physical processes that affect snow depth changes are very complicated.

steps.action: Set three objectives: describe the spatial pattern of mean snow depth and its factors, estimate long-term trends, and relate the trends to local climate and circulation and quantify each factor's contribution.
steps.quote: The three objectives of this study are (a) to analyse the spatial distribution of annual and seasonal mean snow depth

steps.action: Assembled existing data sets: the PMW snow depth product, ERA5 and MERRA2 reanalysis snow depth (derived from SWE/density and depth x cover fraction), CMFD climate forcing, 33 CMA stations, circulation indices and the SRTM DEM.
steps.quote: The PMW data used in this study were developed by Che et al. (2008) and Dai et al. (2017)

steps.action: Fixed the analysis design: Mann-Kendall significance, Theil-Sen slopes, an 11-year Gaussian low-pass filter, Pearson correlation with t tests, standardized multiple linear regression with variance explained, snow year/winter/spring, and an elevation split at 4,000 m.
steps.quote: We applied the nonparametric Mann–Kendall test to detect the statistical significance of the trend in snow depth

steps.action: Mapped annual and seasonal mean snow depth climatologies over the QP for 1980-2018 (Figure 2).
steps.quote: PMW snow depth has the highest mean value in winter (2.65 cm), followed by annual (1.14 cm) and spring (1.04 cm).

steps.action: Compared the PMW climatology with ERA5 and MERRA2: the spatial pattern was similar, but the magnitudes differed strongly.
steps.quote: are similar to the annual and seasonal ERA5 and MERRA2 climatologies of snow depth

steps.action: Fitted spatial linear relations across grid cells between mean PMW snow depth and CMFD air temperature, precipitation and wind speed (Figure 3).
steps.quote: Annually, the mean PMW snow depth shows a negative correlation with air temperature

steps.action: Checked the wind-speed relation separately in the mid- and high-elevation zones (Figure S1, supplement).
steps.quote: annual mean snow depth is significantly (p < .01) negatively correlated with wind speed at both midelevation and high-elevation zones

steps.action: Fitted spatial relations between mean snow depth and elevation and slope (Figure 4).
steps.quote: Annually, there is a significant positive correlation

steps.action: Estimated Theil-Sen trends with Mann-Kendall significance for plateau-mean PMW snow depth, annually and by season, and filtered for multidecadal variability (Figure 5).
steps.quote: The annual mean snow depth in PMW has a significant (p < .10) negative trend

steps.action: Estimated the same trends in ERA5 and MERRA2; these were nonsignificant, a mismatch with PMW.
steps.quote: In ERA5 and MERRA2, the mean snow depth exhibits a nonsignificant (p > .10) trend at both annual and seasonal scales.

steps.action: Estimated grid-wise trends and the fractions of significant negative and positive grids for all three data sets (Figure 6, Table 2).
steps.quote: averaged PMW snow depth is negative for 70.56% of the grids across the QP

steps.action: Chose the PMW data set alone for the influencing-factor analysis, citing the preceding trend analysis.
steps.quote: we selected the PMW dataset to analyse the relationships between snow depth variation and influencing factors

steps.action: Computed trends in CMFD air temperature, precipitation and wind speed over the QP (Figures S2, S3).
steps.quote: air temperature shows a significant (p < .05) increasing trend in snow year

steps.action: Correlated interannual plateau-mean snow depth with the climate variables and the circulation indices (Table 3).
steps.quote: Annually, air temperature exerts the most significant and strongest impact

steps.action: Fitted standardized multiple linear regressions, first on the climate variables and then on the circulation indices, to estimate total and per-factor variance explained.
steps.quote: Annually, air temperature explained 43.85% of snow depth variance

steps.action: Mapped grid-wise correlations and variance explained between snow depth and the climate and circulation factors (Figures 7, 8, S4, S5; Table 4).
steps.quote: annual air temperature correlates negatively with snow depth for 92.75% of the grids in the QP

steps.action: Set the cross-data-set findings (similar pattern, differing magnitudes and trends) against Bian et al. (2020).
steps.quote: consistent with the results of Bian et al. (2020)

steps.action: Proposed post hoc mechanisms for the regional heterogeneity, drawing on cited process studies: elevation-temperature control, sublimation under strong radiation, wind erosion in the open south, and blowing-snow convergence in the Qaidam Basin.
steps.quote: A possible explanation for this phenomenon is that high elevation areas in the southeast and east have colder air temperature and more precipitation

steps.action: Compared the regionally limited AO effect with Zhang et al. (2021e).
steps.quote: being similar to the result of Zhang et al. (2021e)

steps.action: Added the PDO correlation with snow depth (Figure S6); it was nonsignificant in most regions.
steps.quote: This paper also analysed the relationships between PDO and annual and seasonal snow depth in QP (Figure S6)

steps.action: Compared the terrain relations with Bai et al. (2015); there was agreement, but no decrease of snow depth beyond a slope threshold, which the authors attribute to resolution.
steps.quote: This result in Figure 4 is consistent with the research of Bai et al. (2015)

steps.action: Checked the PMW product against station snow depth at the corresponding grids (Figure S7) and against reanalysis snow depth (Figure S8).
steps.quote: Figure S7 shows the spatial distribution of correlation coefficients of station observation snow depth and PMW snow depth on the corresponding grids

steps.action: Kept the claim that air temperature dominates PMW snow depth variation, with regionally varying precipitation, wind and circulation effects.
steps.quote: Air temperature plays a dominant role in modulating total snow depth variation across the QP

end.claim: Over the Qinghai Plateau in 1980-2018, air temperature dominates PMW snow depth variation, explaining 43.85, 24.88 and 47.28% of annual, winter and spring variance, while precipitation, wind and circulation effects are regional.

decisive_move.sentence: The standardized multiple regression of PMW snow depth on the CMFD climate variables, with variance explained per factor, produces the headline attribution to air temperature.

gates.evidence: All data were pre-existing products; no hypothesis directed acquisition. Correlations and trends faced significance tests they could have failed, but no rival explanation was tested, and the reanalyses disagreed on the trends. Nothing was fixed before the data; the regression variable selection admittedly changed the variance explained (p. 1107).

imports.item: Mann-Kendall trend test and Theil-Sen slope estimator
Pearson correlation with Student's t test; multiple linear regression variance decomposition

novelty_claims.quote: [...] studies, the most meaningful difference is that the paper added wind as an influencing factor apart from air temperature and precipitation
few studies examined and quantified the effects of wind on snow depth variation on a large scale

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgement mentions anonymous reviewers, so no review sequence is coded. Other sub-claims sit at other statuses. The PMW trends (annual -0.125 cm/decade at p<.10; spring -0.184 cm/decade at p<.05) are estimate_with_resolution, but ERA5 and MERRA2 do not reproduce them and the paper does not resolve which is right. The circulation effects (AMO, TPRI) are regularity_in_range, limited to localized areas. The physical mechanisms in the Discussion (blowing snow, sublimation, elevation-temperature) are post hoc best explanations, not tested. Attribution rests on correlation and linear regression; the authors note collinearity between temperature and wind, sensitivity to variable selection, and the need for partial correlation or numerical sensitivity experiments, none of which were done. The station validation was announced in Methods but reported only qualitatively, in the Discussion and Figure S7, with spring correlations nonsignificant. Inference: the reason for choosing PMW over the reanalyses for the factor analysis is not stated beyond a reference to the trend analysis. Snowfall was replaced by total precipitation for lack of gridded snowfall data. The 0.25-degree resolution limits the terrain and wind conclusions.

disagreements.target: Bai et al. (2015), snow depth decreasing beyond a slope threshold
disagreements.support: The authors find a monotonic positive snow depth-slope relation at 0.25 degrees and attribute the missing threshold to the coarse resolution.
disagreements.quote: [...] show that snow depth decreases when the slope exceeds a certain range, which might be related to the data resolution

disagreements.target: ERA5 and MERRA2 reanalysis snow depth over the QP
disagreements.support: The reanalyses show no significant trends and differ in magnitude (ERA5 overestimates, MERRA2 underestimates); the authors attribute this to model and forcing uncertainty in a sparsely observed region.
disagreements.quote: make the numerical assimilation models in the region suffer from a high degree of uncertainty
